title: Life Processes in Animals
seo_title: Life Processes in Animals Class 7 Science Worksheet with Answers (NCERT Curiosity Chapter 9)
standard_code: Class 7, Curiosity Chapter 9: Life Processes in Animals
standard_text: Nutrition in animals: the human digestive system, teeth, digestion, absorption, assimilation and egestion; feeding in Amoeba and in ruminants; breathing and respiration, inhaled and exhaled air, breathing organs in different animals (summary of NCERT Curiosity Chapter 9).
meta_desc: Free CBSE Class 7 Science worksheets for NCERT Curiosity Chapter 9: the digestive system, teeth, saliva, bile and villi, Amoeba and ruminants, breathing in and out, exhaled air and breathing organs of animals. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Digestion breaks food into simple substances.
body_html:
How to think about it

Food passes from the mouth through the oesophagus, stomach and small intestine to the large intestine. Saliva starts digesting starch; the stomach's acid and juices act on proteins; bile from the liver breaks fats into droplets; pancreatic juice completes digestion. Villi in the small intestine absorb digested food; the large intestine absorbs water, and waste leaves through the anus.

When we breathe in, the diaphragm moves down and air fills the lungs; exhaled air has more carbon dioxide and turns lime water milky. Cells break down food to release energy (respiration). Fish breathe with gills, earthworms through their skin and insects through spiracles and air tubes.

Example

Where are nutrients absorbed?

villi of the small intestine

Answer: the small intestine

Example

How does an earthworm breathe?

no lungs

Answer: through its moist skin

Common mistakes

  • Thinking digestion starts in the stomach.
  • Thinking exhaled air is pure carbon dioxide.
  • Saying bile digests proteins.

faq.q: What is the role of villi?
faq.a: They are finger-like folds of the small intestine that give a large surface to absorb digested food into the blood.

faq.q: How is exhaled air different from inhaled air?
faq.a: It has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide and water vapour.

items.q: What is the job of the mouth in digestion?
c: chewing food and mixing it with saliva
churning food with acid and digestive juices that break down proteins
completing digestion and absorbing nutrients into the blood
making pancreatic juice that digests carbohydrates, proteins and fats
items.e: The mouth: chewing food and mixing it with saliva.

items.q: Where does the digestion of starch begin?
items.e: Chew a piece of roti for a while; it tastes sweet.

items.q: Which part of the digestive system is responsible for making bile, which helps digest fats?
items.e: The liver: making bile, which helps digest fats.

items.q: Which part of the digestive system is responsible for chewing food and mixing it with saliva?
items.e: The mouth: chewing food and mixing it with saliva.

items.q: What are villi?
c: finger-like projections in the small intestine that absorb digested food
items.e: They give a large surface area.

items.q: Which part of the digestive system is responsible for completing digestion and absorbing nutrients into the blood?
items.e: The small intestine: completing digestion and absorbing nutrients into the blood.

items.q: What is the job of the pancreas in digestion?
c: completing digestion and absorbing nutrients into the blood
making bile, which helps digest fats
absorbing water and some salts from undigested food
making pancreatic juice that digests carbohydrates, proteins and fats
items.e: The pancreas: making pancreatic juice that digests carbohydrates, proteins and fats.

items.q: What happens when we breathe in?
c: the chest expands, the diaphragm moves down and air fills the lungs
items.e: This is inhalation.

items.q: What is egestion?
c: removing undigested food from the body through the anus
items.e: It is the last step of digestion.

items.q: Why do we sneeze?
c: to push out dust or irritants from the nose
items.e: Cover your mouth when you sneeze.

items.q: What is the role of the tongue in digestion?
c: it mixes food with saliva and pushes it back for swallowing
items.e: It also tastes the food.

items.q: Which part of the digestive system is responsible for making saliva, which begins to digest starch?
items.e: The salivary glands: making saliva, which begins to digest starch.

items.q: Why does the nose have hairs and mucus?
c: to trap dust and germs from the air we breathe
items.e: Breathe through the nose, not the mouth.

items.q: Why should we chew food properly?
c: small pieces mix better with saliva and are digested easily
items.e: Chewing is the first step of digestion.

completing digestion and absorbing nutrients into the blood

items.e: The stomach: churning food with acid and digestive juices that break down proteins.

items.q: Which part of the digestive system is responsible for carrying food from the mouth to the stomach?
items.e: The oesophagus (food pipe): carrying food from the mouth to the stomach.

items.e: The pancreas: making pancreatic juice that digests carbohydrates, proteins and fats.

items.q: What is digestion?
c: breaking down complex food into simple substances the body can absorb
items.e: It happens in the digestive tract.

items.q: Why does the stomach make hydrochloric acid?
c: it kills germs and helps digestive juices act on proteins
items.e: Mucus protects the stomach wall from the acid.

items.q: Which kind of food does pancreatic juice act on?
c: the final breakdown of all kinds of food into simple substances
items.e: Pancreatic juice: carbohydrates, proteins and fats.

items.q: Which teeth are used for tearing food?
items.e: Canines: tearing food.

items.q: Which teeth are used for grinding food with their broad surfaces?
items.e: Molars: grinding food with their broad surfaces.

items.q: Which digestive juice acts on starch, changing it into sugar?
items.e: Saliva: starch, changing it into sugar.

items.q: How does an Amoeba take in food?
c: it surrounds the food with finger-like projections (pseudopodia) and forms a food vacuole
items.e: Digestion happens in the food vacuole.

items.q: What are premolars used for?
c: grinding food with their broad surfaces
items.e: Premolars: chewing and grinding food.

items.q: What is assimilation?
c: the body using absorbed food to build new parts and get energy
items.e: Cells use glucose and amino acids.

items.q: Why do we breathe faster after running?
c: the muscles need more oxygen to release more energy
items.e: The breathing rate rises with exercise.

items.q: Which digestive juice acts on carbohydrates, proteins and fats?

items.q: Which digestive juice acts on proteins?

items.e: Humans pass cellulose out as fibre.

items.q: What are canines used for?

items.q: Which organ does a frog breathe with?
items.e: A frog: lungs and its moist skin.

items.q: Why do we sometimes get cramps after hard exercise?
c: muscles release energy without enough oxygen and lactic acid builds up
items.e: Rest and a gentle massage help.

items.q: What is the job of the oesophagus (food pipe) in digestion?

items.e: The oesophagus (food pipe): carrying food from the mouth to the stomach.

items.q: Which organ does a human breathe with?

items.q: Which of these is not true of the air we breathe in?
c: it does not turn lime water milky quickly
it is usually cooler than our body
it has less water vapour than exhaled air
items.e: It has more carbon dioxide: not true of the air we breathe in. The other three are.

items.q: Which part of the digestive system is responsible for storing undigested waste for a short time?
items.e: The rectum: storing undigested waste for a short time.

items.q: What is the cud?
c: partly digested food brought back from the rumen to the mouth for chewing
items.e: Ruminants chew the cud while resting.
